questions.question: In crypto code, why is comparing secrets with a naive equality check risky?
options: Because equality checks can leak information through timing differences (early exit on mismatch)
Because equality checks change the value being compared due to encoding conversions
Because equality checks are non-deterministic and may return different results each run
Because equality checks can be reversed to recover the secret without any oracle
questions.explanation: Many naive comparisons stop at the first mismatch, so runtime can correlate with how many prefix bytes were correct.

questions.question: Which of these is the best default in Python when comparing a server-computed MAC/tag to attacker-provided bytes?
options: `hmac.compare_digest(expected, provided)`
`expected == provided`
`expected.hex() == provided.hex()`
`expected.startswith(provided)`
questions.explanation: `hmac.compare_digest` is designed to avoid content-based short-circuiting and is the right default for tag comparisons.

questions.question: What does “constant-time” mean in the context of defending against timing side channels?
options: The runtime does not depend on secret data (though it may depend on public lengths/parameters)
The runtime is exactly the same number of CPU cycles for all possible inputs and lengths
The code never uses loops, so it cannot leak timing information
The algorithm has O(1) time complexity for all input sizes
questions.explanation: Security constant-time means “no secret-dependent timing”, not “O(1) complexity” and not “identical for all lengths”.

questions.question: Which code pattern is most directly vulnerable to a prefix timing leak?
options: Loop over bytes and `return False` immediately on the first mismatch
Compute `diff |= a[i] ^ b[i]` for all bytes and decide equality at the end
Decode base64 strictly (reject whitespace and non-canonical padding)
Hash the message and compare the resulting digest lengths
questions.explanation: Early return on mismatch makes runtime correlate with the mismatch position, leaking how many prefix bytes were correct.

questions.question: Why is comparing presentation strings (hex/base64) often worse than comparing bytes for secret checks?
options: Multiple encodings can represent the same bytes (non-canonical forms), and string compares can introduce extra leaks
Hex and base64 are encrypted, so comparing them is equivalent to decrypting secrets
String comparison always runs in constant time in Python, so it hides bugs
Bytes cannot be compared in Python, only strings can
questions.explanation: Decode strictly to bytes at the boundary, enforce canonical forms, then compare bytes with a timing-resistant routine.

questions.question: A constant-time-style compare still does an explicit length check. When is it generally acceptable for the length check to be “fast”?
options: When the compared values have a protocol-fixed, public length (e.g., a 32-byte tag)
Never — any length check is always a catastrophic secret leak
Only when comparing user-visible strings like usernames
Only when the compared values are both empty
questions.explanation: If length is public and fixed by the protocol, a fast reject on length mismatch is usually fine; the main risk is leaking content.

questions.question: In a classic timing attack against MAC verification with early-exit comparison, what does the attacker learn from response time?
options: How many leading bytes of the provided tag matched the expected tag
The secret key used to compute the MAC in a single request
The full expected tag instantly without brute force
A collision in the underlying hash function
questions.explanation: Early-exit comparisons leak where the first mismatch occurs, which is enough to brute-force the next byte iteratively.

questions.question: What is the safest practical advice for production cryptographic comparisons in this course?
options: Use audited library primitives (e.g., `hmac.compare_digest`) rather than rolling your own constant-time compare in Python
Implement your own compare with XOR/OR loops and assume it is constant-time everywhere
Use `time.sleep()` to “pad” the runtime until it looks constant
Convert everything to integers and compare integer values with `==`
questions.explanation: Constant-time properties are subtle. In production, prefer audited, widely used constant-time primitives provided by standard libraries.
